frontmatter_description: Diagnose why and how a character controls outward emotional expression because a social display rule, role expectation, or situational norm requires it.
title: Emotional Disguise and Display Rules
use_when: Use when the question asks why a character smiles, stays calm, hides disappointment, acts pleased, or otherwise manages emotional expression for politeness, professionalism, safety, ceremony, or role expectations.
Use when the key issue is not merely what the person feels, but what social rule determines what they should show.
Use when outward emotion is shaped by audience, setting, relationship, status, or occasion.
Use when explaining a deliberate or learned expression-control strategy such as masking, softening, exaggerating, neutralizing, or substituting an emotion.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the task only asks to NAME the true feeling behind a contrary display, without asking why the display is socially controlled; that is the detect-the-mismatch capability - identifying the hidden inner feeling (micro-28).

Do not use when the character actually CHANGES the inner feeling - reappraising the situation, calming down, or shifting attention - rather than just controlling the outward expression; that is the emotion-regulation capability (micro-33).
Do not use when the emotion itself is surprising or nonstandard but there is no rule-based expression management; that is the atypical-emotion capability (micro-27).
Do not use when guilt, shame, pride, gratitude, blame, or moral responsibility is the central cause of the emotion; that is the moral-emotion capability (micro-30).
Do not use when the display is accidental leakage, a spontaneous facial cue, or a physiological reaction rather than deliberately controlled expression.
decision_variable: the social display rule governing expression
trigger_checklist: Is there a mismatch, adjustment, or filtering between felt emotion and shown emotion?
Is the adjustment motivated by a social rule, role, audience, occasion, politeness norm, or expectation?
Can the character identify who is present and what expression would be acceptable or unacceptable there?
Does the answer require explaining the outward display rather than only naming the inner feeling?
Would the display change if the audience, setting, or role changed?
workflow: Confirm the question asks WHY the character shows a particular expression (or why they keep it under control), not merely what they feel inside.
Identify the character's likely internal emotion from events, goals, and appraisal.
Identify the audience, relationship, setting, role, or occasion that creates a display expectation.
State the relevant display rule, such as being polite to a host, staying calm as a leader, not gloating in front of a loser, protecting someone's feelings, or smiling for a photo.
Name the expression-control tactic the character uses: hide, soften, exaggerate, replace, or neutralize the shown emotion.

Answer with the social reason for the controlled display. Note that the inner feeling persists - if the character had instead TALKED THEMSELVES OUT of the feeling, that would be the emotion-regulation capability (micro-33), not a display rule.

special_case.title: Composed display driven by a social role
special_case.rule: When a person's role or audience makes a particular expression expected (a leader stays composed, a host stays gracious, a winner does not gloat), the outward emotion is governed by that display rule even though the true feeling differs.

worked_example.scene: Zhao Bo is the president of the skateboard club. While demonstrating in front of the members, he falls and gets hurt. He keeps a confident face instead of showing pain or embarrassment.
worked_example.question: Why does Zhao Bo appear confident on the surface?
worked_example.answer_logic: Zhao Bo privately feels embarrassed, but as club president he is expected to project competence and keep the members' trust. The display rule of his leadership role drives the confident face; that social reason - not the inner embarrassment - is the answer. (If the question had asked what he really feels, the answer would be embarrassed, which is the detect-the-mismatch capability instead.)

boundary_exit_rule: If the question can be answered by naming the hidden true emotion without explaining a social rule for the outward expression, exit to the detect-the-mismatch capability - identifying the true inner feeling (micro-28).
If the character changes the feeling itself through reappraisal, calming, or attention shift rather than controlling the display, exit to the emotion-regulation capability (micro-33).
If the central puzzle is why the true emotion is unusual for the situation, exit to the atypical-emotion capability (micro-27).
If the central appraisal is responsibility, wrongdoing, deservedness, or norm violation, exit to the moral-emotion capability (micro-30).
If the expression is primarily a communicative signal such as a wink, glance, or gesture meant to convey an intention, route to the relevant communication or nonverbal-intention capability instead.

references.route_signal: Use this micro unit when a character's outward emotion is strategically shaped by a display rule tied to politeness, role, audience, or situation.
hard_boundary: This unit is about rule-governed expression control, not all hidden emotion.
The decisive evidence must include a display norm or social expectation.

The answer must NAME the social display rule driving the outward expression; the inner feeling may be referenced as context but is not the answer itself (the bare inner feeling is the detect-the-mismatch capability, micro-28).
Do not infer deception automatically; many display rules are polite, protective, professional, or ceremonial rather than dishonest.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not assume the displayed emotion is the true emotion just because it is visible.
Do not label every smile as happiness; check whether the social setting rewards that display.
Do not give the bare inner feeling when the question asks WHY the person manages the expression - that bare-feeling answer is the detect-the-mismatch capability (micro-28), not this unit.
Do not over-moralize polite masking as lying unless truthfulness or intent to mislead is the main issue.
common_failure_modes: Answering with the bare inner feeling and omitting the social display rule the question is really asking for.
Ignoring the audience and treating the expression as purely personal.
Confusing rule-governed display control with actually changing the feeling (emotion regulation).
Confusing emotional disguise with an atypical emotion.
Treating culturally or role-specific display expectations as universal without using scene evidence.

minimal_pair.case: Chen Fei wins a card game but keeps a calm face; asked WHY he appears calm, the answer is 'to avoid upsetting his friend.'
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The question targets the social reason for the managed display - a do-not-gloat politeness rule - which is exactly this unit.

minimal_pair.case: Same Chen Fei scene, but asked 'What are Chen Fei's real feelings?' the answer is 'happy.'
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: This routes to the detect-the-mismatch capability (micro-28): it asks only for the bare inner feeling, with no social rule needed.

boundary_stress_test: Zhao Bo, a club president, hides pain after falling to keep a confident face: the leadership role is the display rule, so this unit applies when the question asks why he looks confident.
If a contestant smiles after losing, check whether sportsmanship or public-facing expectations govern the expression rather than genuine happiness - if so, this unit applies.
If a slighted boy tells himself he is a 'secret weapon' and turns to the next game, route to the emotion-regulation capability (micro-33): he changes the feeling, he does not just control a display.
If someone laughs at bad news because of a genuinely unusual appraisal, route to the atypical-emotion capability (micro-27) unless a display rule explains the laugh.
If someone apologizes and feels guilt, route to the moral-emotion capability (micro-30) when responsibility appraisal is the central variable, even if they also control their face.
references.generalization_note: Display rules vary by culture, role, relationship, and situation, but the operational pattern is stable: infer the felt emotion, identify the social expectation, and explain the controlled outward display - while the inner feeling itself stays unchanged.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: A person feels one emotion but shows another because politeness, professionalism, ceremony, status, role, or audience expectations make that display appropriate; the question asks WHY they show it.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: The same masked scene, but the question asks only for the bare true feeling; with no social rule needed, it routes to the detect-the-mismatch capability.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The character changes the inner feeling itself (reappraisal, attention shift), which routes to the emotion-regulation capability; or guilt/responsibility is central, routing to the moral-emotion capability.

notes: Keep the unit focused on the social rule governing emotional display, not on broad deception or emotion recognition.
Decisive test against the detect-the-mismatch capability: that unit answers WHAT is felt; this unit answers WHY the display is managed.
Decisive test against emotion regulation: here the feeling persists and only the display is controlled; there the feeling itself is changed.
Use concise explanations that name the inner emotion, the display rule, and the controlled outward expression.
core_question: Explain why and how a character manages outward emotion for politeness, role, or situation
